t: Death certificates: how many to order and who needs one
pre: Most families end up needing more than they expect.

b.p: Almost every account, policy and agency your family deals with will ask for proof of death. Many want a certified copy, not a photocopy. A certified copy is an official copy ordered from the vital records office (or through the funeral home), with a raised or printed seal, and some keep the copy for good.

Many families order 5 to 10 certified copies. Families with a house, several bank accounts, life insurance or a pension often lean toward 10. Ordering extras at the start is cheaper and faster than going back for more later.

list: Life insurance companies
Banks, brokerages and retirement account providers
Pension plans and employers
The county recorder, to retitle a house
The DMV, to transfer a car
The probate court, if there's probate
The Social Security Administration, in some cases

b.p: The funeral home usually orders the first batch for you, and it's the easiest time to do it. Later, you can order more from the vital records office in the state or county where the death happened. Cost is usually $10 to $30 per copy, and it varies by state.

b.tip: Many places will accept a photocopy if asked. Families who check first often save their certified copies for the places that insist on one.

t: The phone plan: don't close it too soon
pre: One phone number can unlock dozens of accounts.

b.p: It's natural to want to cancel a phone plan quickly. But for many people, their phone number is the key to their accounts. Banks, email and apps text a code to that number before they'll let anyone in.
If the line is shut off, those codes stop arriving, and getting into accounts can turn into weeks of calls and paperwork.

steps: Many families keep the line active for at least 3 to 6 months, or until the accounts are closed or transferred.
It helps to keep the phone charged and somewhere safe, along with its passcode.
If the phone is on a family plan, the account holder can usually keep it running. Policies vary by carrier, so it's worth a call.
If you'd like to keep the number for good, most carriers can transfer it into your name.

b.h: What to write in your binder

list: Which carrier the phone is with
Whose name the account is in
The account PIN or passcode, if there is one

b.tip: Changing the voicemail greeting can wait. Some families keep the original greeting for years, and that's okay.

t: Pets: who takes them?
pre: A name and a backup name. That's most of it.

b.p: If something happened to you tomorrow, who would feed your pets tonight? Writing down one answer takes a minute, and it saves your family a hard guess in a hard week.

list: Who takes each pet, and a backup in case they can't
Your vet's name and phone number
Food, medications and any health conditions
Anything that helps, like "hides under the bed with strangers" or "only eats the chicken flavor"

b.p: Many people check with the person before putting their name down. A pet can be a big commitment, and it's easier on everyone to find out now than to surprise them later.

You can mention pets in your will, and every state now allows a pet trust, which sets money aside for a pet's care. The rules for setting one up vary by state. Both are optional. A clear note in your binder already covers what most families need.

b.tip: A small card in your wallet that says "I have pets at home" with a contact name means someone will check on them quickly if you're ever in an accident.

t: Do I need a will? What happens if you don't have one
pre: Without one, your state decides.

b.p: A will says who gets your things and who's in charge of sorting them out. If you don't have one, you haven't avoided those decisions. Your state's default rules make them for you.

list: State law decides who inherits. Usually that's a spouse and children first (in many states they share), then parents, then brothers and sisters. The split varies a lot by state, especially in community-property states and blended families.
A court picks the person who handles your estate.
If you have children under 18, a court decides who raises them.
Unmarried partners, stepchildren and close friends usually get nothing by default.

b.p: Some things pass outside a will: life insurance, retirement accounts, and bank accounts with a named beneficiary, plus anything owned jointly. Those go to whoever is on the form, no matter what the will says.

list: Parents of children under 18
Anyone who owns a home
Unmarried couples
Blended families
Anyone who wants something to go to a specific person

b.tip: The exact default rules vary by state. Searching "[your state] intestate succession" shows who would inherit where you live.

t: Affordable ways to make a will
pre: A basic will doesn't have to cost much.

b.p: If your situation is straightforward, you have several low-cost options. The key is that the will is signed and witnessed the way your state requires.

table: Simple situations; guides you through state rules
Your state's fill-in form (a few states offer one)
Many benefits packages cover a will at no cost
Legal aid or a law school clinic
Kids, a house, a business, or anything complicated

b.p: Most states require you to sign in front of two or more witnesses, usually people who don't inherit anything. A few states allow other options, such as notarization. Many also let you add a notarized form (often called a self-proving affidavit) that makes probate easier later. Some states accept a fully handwritten will, but many don't, so don't count on it.

b.h: When to pay for a lawyer

b.p: People often use one if they have a blended family, a child with special needs, a business, property in more than one state, or someone likely to challenge the will.

b.tip: Once it's signed, write down where the original is kept. A will your family can't find doesn't help anyone.

t: Will vs. trust: what's the difference?
pre: Both pass things on. They take different routes.

b.p: A will and a living trust both say who gets what. The big difference is how things get there, and whether a court is involved.

table: No, if it's set up fully
No, you still need a will for this
You have to move assets into it

b.p: A trust only controls what's in it. If the house or bank accounts are never retitled into the trust's name, they may still go through probate. This step is called funding the trust, and it's the one people most often skip.

A will is enough for many people. A trust is often worth it if you own a home, especially in a state where probate is slow or costly, own property in more than one state, or want privacy or more control over when people inherit.

b.tip: Most people with a trust also have a short will, called a pour-over will, that catches anything left outside the trust.

t: Power of attorney, in plain English
pre: Who handles things if you can't?

b.p: A power of attorney (POA) is a document that lets someone you trust act for you while you're alive but unable to, for example after an accident or during a serious illness. It isn't about what happens after death.

b.h: The two kinds most people need

list: Financial power of attorney: lets your chosen person pay bills, manage bank accounts and handle taxes.
Healthcare power of attorney (also called a healthcare proxy): lets them make medical decisions if you can't speak for yourself.
Durable: it keeps working if you become unable to decide for yourself. This is the kind you want.
Springing: it only starts once a doctor confirms you can't decide. It sounds safer, but it can cause delays.
Agent: the person you choose.

b.p: Your family may have to go to court to get guardianship or conservatorship before they can pay your bills or talk to your bank. That can take months and cost thousands.
Every POA ends at death. After that, the executor named in your will takes over. They're two separate roles in two separate documents, though many people pick the same person for both.

b.tip: Some banks prefer their own POA form. It's worth asking your bank whether they'll accept yours, so there are no surprises.

t: What's a healthcare directive, and how do I make one?
pre: Free, about 20 minutes, and a huge gift to your family.

b.p: A healthcare directive (also called an advance directive) tells doctors and your family what care you'd want if you couldn't speak for yourself. It takes a very hard decision off their shoulders.

list: A living will: your wishes about treatments like life support, feeding tubes and resuscitation.
A healthcare proxy: the person who speaks for you with doctors.

b.p: Names and forms vary by state. Some states combine both parts into one form, and some use a separate form (often called a POLST) for people who are seriously ill.

steps: Getting the state's free form. Searching "[your state] advance directive form" finds it, and doctors and hospitals usually have copies.
Choosing a healthcare proxy and talking with them first, so they know what you want.
Filling it in. Plain words are fine.
Signing it the way the state requires. Most states need two witnesses or a notary.
Giving copies to the proxy and the doctor, and keeping one in the binder.

b.p: You don't need a lawyer for this. Many hospitals and senior centers will help you fill it in for free.
A directive from one state isn't always honored in another. If you move, or spend a lot of time in another state, it's worth filling in that state's form too.

b.tip: Talking it through with your proxy matters as much as the form. A 15-minute conversation now can save your family days of doubt.

t: No will, trust or directive yet? Where to start
pre: You're in good company. Here's the easy order.

b.p: Most adults don't have these documents yet. In a 2025 Caring.com survey, only 24% of US adults said they had a will. Writing "None" in your template is honest and useful: it tells your family where things stand, and it gives you a clear list of what to do next.

b.h: One reasonable order to tackle them

steps: Healthcare directive. It's free, takes about 20 minutes, and your state has a form.
Checking beneficiaries. Many people look at whether their life insurance and retirement accounts still name the right people. It usually takes a few minutes online.
Financial power of attorney. Often free or cheap, and it keeps your family out of court if you're ever unable to decide.
Will. An online service works for many people, and a lawyer is worth it if things are complicated.
Trust, if it makes sense. Worth considering if you own a home or want to avoid probate.

b.p: You don't have to do them all this month. Even doing just the first two covers a lot.

b.tip: Many people come back and change "None" to where each document is kept once it's done. It's often the first line family looks for.

t: Print backup codes for your email
pre: A short list of codes that opens the door when the phone can't.

b.p: Most email accounts send a code to your phone before they let anyone sign in. If the phone is lost, locked or shut off, that code never arrives. Backup codes are the way around it: a handful of one-time codes the email provider gives you in advance.

Email is where password resets go. If your family can get into your email, they can usually reset the passwords for most of your other accounts. If they can't, every account becomes its own phone call.

list: Gmail: a set of backup codes (currently 10, each 8 digits), each usable once. They're in your Google Account under Security, then 2-Step Verification.
Outlook and Microsoft accounts: several recovery options, including a recovery code, found in the account's security settings.
Apple (iCloud Mail): an optional recovery key. If you turn it on, it replaces some of Apple's usual recovery steps, so losing it can make things harder.

b.p: Menu names change from time to time. Searching "[your email provider] backup codes" usually finds the current steps.

Google's own help pages suggest printing the codes or writing them down and keeping them somewhere safe. People who use a binder sometimes keep them there, alongside the email address they belong to; others keep them in a password manager or a locked drawer. Unlike a code texted to your phone, these are printed in advance, and each one on the list can only be used once. Some people cross a code off after using it, so they know how many are left.

b.tip: Getting a new set of backup codes from Google or Microsoft usually cancels the old codes. If you get new ones, replace the old list wherever you keep it.

t: Two-factor codes, in plain English
pre: The second lock on an account, and why it trips families up.

b.p: Two-factor sign-in (sometimes called 2FA or two-step verification) means an account asks for two things: your password, plus a second proof that it's really you. That second proof is usually a short code.

list: A text message to your phone number
An authenticator app on your phone, such as Google Authenticator or Microsoft Authenticator
A pop-up on your phone asking "Is this you?"
A small physical key that plugs into a computer or taps a phone

b.h: Why it matters for your family

b.p: Two-factor sign-in is very good at keeping strangers out. It also keeps your family out. Even with every password written down, they may still need the phone, its passcode, or a backup code to get in.

b.h: What families usually need to know

list: Which accounts use it
Where the codes arrive (which phone number or which app)
Where any backup codes are kept

b.p: Keeping this extra security on is fine. What helps your family most is a note saying where the codes go.

b.tip: Authenticator apps live on one phone. If that phone is reset or replaced, the codes can disappear with it unless the app has a backup or sync feature turned on.

t: How to find which accounts use two-factor codes
pre: A few places to look, about 15 minutes.

b.p: Most people don't remember which accounts ask for a code. The good news is that the list is usually hiding in a few predictable places.

steps: Your authenticator app. Every account it lists uses two-factor sign-in.
Your text messages. Searching for "code" or "verification" shows which companies text you codes.
Your password manager, if you use one. Many flag which saved accounts have two-factor sign-in turned on.
Your email. Searching for "verification code" or "sign-in code" finds accounts that email codes instead.
The big accounts directly. Your email, bank, Apple or Google account and mobile carrier each show it in their security settings.

b.p: For each account, a short line is enough: the account name, where the code goes, and where any backup codes are kept. For example: "Chase: text to my cell. No backup codes."
If the list feels long, many people start with email, banking and the phone carrier, since those tend to unlock the rest.

b.tip: If an account texts codes to your phone number, that's one more reason your family might keep the phone line active for a while.

t: Where to find your routing and account numbers
pre: They're on the bottom of a paper check and in your bank's app.

b.p: Every bank account has two numbers that matter: a routing number, which identifies the bank, and an account number, which identifies your account. Your family uses them to find the account and set up transfers.
They're along the bottom edge. The first group, a 9-digit number, is the routing number. The next group is the account number. The last, shorter group is the check number.

list: Your bank's app or website, usually under account details
A monthly paper or PDF statement
A direct deposit form from your bank
Calling the number on the back of your debit card
Some banks use a different routing number for wire transfers. If there's one listed, it's worth writing both down.
The account number on your debit card is not your bank account number. The card has its own number.
Routing numbers are public. Any bank's routing number can be looked up on its website.

b.tip: In the binder, many people write just the bank name, the type of account and the last four digits. Banks can usually find a deceased customer's accounts without the full account number, so it can stay out of sight.

t: Is it safe to write account numbers down?
pre: Mostly yes, with a few sensible limits.

b.p: Writing your account numbers on paper sounds risky, but those numbers already travel a lot. Your account number is printed on every check you've ever written. What matters more is what's written next to them.

list: Bank name and account type
The last four digits of each account
Routing numbers, which are public anyway
Online banking passwords written on the same page
Full card numbers along with the expiration date and security code
Your Social Security number on the same page

b.p: A common middle ground is to write the bank name and last four digits in the binder, and keep full numbers and passwords somewhere more secure, like a password manager or a locked drawer. After a death, banks usually identify accounts by the customer's full name and Social Security number, along with a death certificate and paperwork showing who's in charge of the estate. The full account number usually isn't needed. Requirements vary by bank.
Where the binder lives matters more than what's in it. A binder in a locked or out-of-sight place is a very different risk from one on the kitchen counter.

b.tip: If a binder with account numbers is ever lost or stolen, banks can usually close the account and open a new one with a different number. And if you filled in your Just In Case templates in Google Drive, your whole plan is still there. You can print a new binder in minutes.

t: How to put a beneficiary on file
pre: A short form that can matter more than your will.

b.p: Many accounts let you name a beneficiary: the person who receives the account when you die. When there's a named beneficiary, the account usually goes straight to them without probate court, and it goes to them even if your will says something else.

table: Insurer or HR, for work policies
Cars and homes, in some states

steps: Online, beneficiaries are usually under a "beneficiaries" section in the account settings. In person, a bank teller or branch staff can usually help with the form on the spot. The number on the back of the card is another option.
The form asks for each person's full name. Some also ask for a birth date or Social Security number.
Many forms let you name a backup, called a contingent beneficiary, in case the first person dies first.
Many people save the confirmation and note in their binder who's named on each account.

list: For a 401(k), federal law generally makes your spouse the beneficiary unless they sign a written waiver. IRAs generally don't have this federal rule.
In community-property states, a spouse may have rights to part of an account even if someone else is named.
Transfer-on-death deeds for homes and TOD titles for cars are only available in some states.

b.tip: Life changes like marriage, divorce or a new baby are common times to check these forms. For work plans like a 401(k) or employer life insurance, federal law generally pays whoever is on the form, even an ex-spouse. For individual policies, about half of states automatically remove an ex after divorce.

t: How to find all your accounts
pre: The forgotten ones are the ones families lose.

b.p: Most people can name their main checking account. The accounts that get lost are the old ones: a 401(k) from a job years ago, a savings account opened for a promotion, a brokerage account nobody checks.

steps: Your email. Searching for "statement", "account" or "tax form" turns up banks and brokerages that still send mail.
Last year's tax return. Most 1099 and 1098 forms point to an account.
Your credit report. It lists credit cards and loans. It's free from AnnualCreditReport.com, the official site.
Old jobs. Each past employer may have a retirement plan with your name on it.
Your bank statements. Regular transfers out often point to another account.

b.p: The US Department of Labor runs a free Retirement Savings Lost and Found database that can help find plans from former employers. Searching "Retirement Savings Lost and Found" finds it.
Accounts left untouched for years are usually handed to the state as unclaimed property. MissingMoney.com searches many states at once, and each state also has its own free search.

b.tip: Writing down accounts you've closed helps too. It saves your family from chasing an account that no longer exists.

t: What happens to a mortgage when someone dies?
pre: The loan doesn't disappear, and the house usually isn't taken right away.

b.p: A mortgage doesn't end when the borrower dies. The loan stays attached to the house, and someone has to keep paying it, sell the house, or let the lender take it back.

list: The estate is responsible for the loan, not the family members personally, unless someone co-signed or was a co-borrower.
Payments are still due each month, and lenders can start foreclosure if they stop.
Whoever inherits the house can usually keep it by continuing the payments, refinancing, or paying the loan off.

b.p: A federal law, the Garn-St Germain Act, generally stops a lender from demanding the full balance just because a home passes to a relative after a death. It covers homes with fewer than five units, including co-op units and manufactured homes, but not commercial property or larger buildings.

Federal mortgage rules from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau also require most lenders to talk to a family member who inherits the house (called a successor in interest) and share information about the loan.

b.h: What families find useful to know

list: Which lender holds the mortgage, and the loan number
Whether anyone else is on the loan
Whether there's mortgage life insurance or a reverse mortgage, since both work differently

b.tip: Reverse mortgages usually come due when the borrower dies. Heirs typically have a set window to repay, sell or hand the house back. Rules depend on the loan.

t: Co-signers: what happens to a loan when someone dies
pre: The co-signer usually still owes it.

b.p: Co-signing means agreeing to pay a loan if the main borrower doesn't. That promise usually stays in place after a death. If one person on the loan dies, the other is generally still responsible for the full balance.

table: Depends on the loan terms; some lenders release co-signers, some don't
Some contracts let the lender demand full repayment. Many lenders have dropped this, but no federal law requires it
Discharged; no one owes it. Parent PLUS loans are also discharged if the student dies
Most federal loans don't use co-signers. PLUS loans can have an endorser, which works similarly
Other account holder owes the balance
Other account holder owes the balance

b.p: Someone who's only an authorized user on a credit card usually doesn't owe the balance. The debt belongs to the account holder's estate.

b.h: What families find useful to know

list: Every loan with a co-signer, and who it is
The lender and account number
Whether the loan has any death or disability coverage

b.tip: Debt collectors sometimes contact family members who don't owe anything. Under federal rules, relatives generally aren't responsible for a family member's debts unless they co-signed, were a joint account holder, or live in a community-property state where different rules can apply.

t: What happens to a car loan when someone dies
pre: The car and the loan go together.

b.p: When someone dies with a car loan, the loan becomes a debt of their estate. The lender still holds the title until it's paid off, so the car can't be sold or transferred without dealing with the loan.

list: Keeping up payments. Whoever inherits the car can often keep making the payments. Some lenders let them take over the loan, and others ask them to refinance in their own name.
Paying it off. The estate pays the balance, often from savings or life insurance, and the title is released.
Selling the car. The sale pays off the loan, and anything left goes to the estate.
Returning it. If no one wants the car, the lender can take it back. If it sells for less than is owed, the estate may still owe the difference.

b.p: If there's a co-signer, they're usually responsible for the payments.
A lease is a rental contract, not a loan. Some leasing companies end the lease early after a death, and others expect payments to continue. The lease agreement says which.

b.tip: Some car loans come with credit life insurance, which can pay off part or all of the loan after a death. It's often listed in the loan paperwork. GAP coverage is different: it pays the shortfall if the car is totaled or stolen, not because the borrower died.

t: List your auto-paid bills
pre: The bills nobody sees are the ones that keep charging.

b.p: Auto-pay is easy to set up and easy to forget. After a death, those payments usually keep going until someone stops them, and some, like insurance and utilities, need to keep going for a while.

list: Bank statements: recurring withdrawals each month
Credit card statements: subscriptions and memberships
Your bank's bill pay screen
Your phone's app store subscriptions (Apple or Google)
PayPal and similar payment apps

b.h: Bills families usually keep paying at first

list: Mortgage or rent
Home and car insurance
Utilities: power, water, gas
The phone line
Health insurance for anyone still covered by the plan
Streaming services
Gym memberships
Magazine and app subscriptions
Club and charity memberships

b.p: For each bill, a short line covers it: what it is, roughly how much, the date it comes out, and which account or card pays it. For example: "Electric, about $120, the 15th, Chase checking."

b.tip: When a bank account is frozen after a death, auto-payments from it may stop without warning. Knowing which bills come from which account helps your family catch the important ones.

t: No accountant, lawyer or advisor? What to write instead
pre: Most people don't have one. That's useful to know too.

b.p: The template asks for your accountant, lawyer and financial advisor. Many people don't have any of them, and writing "None" is a real answer. It tells your family they won't find a professional who already knows your situation.

list: Who does your taxes: yourself with software (and which one), a tax prep chain, or a friend
Where past tax returns are kept
Any lawyer you've used before, even once, for a house closing or a will
Any bank or brokerage contact you've spoken with

b.h: Where families often find help later

list: Probate court self-help centers, which many counties run for free
Legal aid offices, for people with limited income
Your state bar association's lawyer referral service, which often offers a low-cost first meeting
IRS Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA), which prepares returns for free for people who qualify

b.tip: If you write "None" now, you can come back and add a name if you ever hire someone.

t: Where to find your policy number and coverage amount
pre: Usually on the first page of the policy.

b.p: Your family needs two things to file a life insurance claim: the insurance company's name and the policy number. The coverage amount, also called the death benefit or face amount, tells them what to expect.

list: The policy documents, usually on the first page or the page labeled "Policy data" or "Schedule"
The insurer's app or website
Annual statements, which many insurers mail each year
Your bank statements, which show the premium payments and the company name
Your employer's benefits portal, for coverage through work

b.h: If no one can find the policy

b.p: The National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) runs a free Life Insurance Policy Locator. After a death, a family member can submit a request, and participating insurers check their records and contact the beneficiary if they find a policy.

list: Insurance company and phone number
Policy number
Type: term, whole, or through work
Coverage amount
Who the beneficiaries are

b.tip: Some policies come with extras, like a payment for accidental death. These are called riders and are listed in the policy.

t: Term vs. whole life, in plain English
pre: One is for a set number of years. The other is for life.

b.p: Most life insurance falls into two types. The main difference is how long the coverage lasts, and what you pay for it.

table: A set period, often 10, 20 or 30 years
Your whole life, as long as premiums are paid
Much higher for the same coverage
Yes, a savings part that grows slowly
Not applicable; it pays whenever you die

b.p: People often choose term life to cover years when others depend on their income, such as while children are young or a mortgage is being paid. Whole life is often chosen by people who want coverage that never ends or who want the savings feature.

list: Universal life: a type of permanent insurance with more flexible premiums
Group life: coverage through an employer, usually term
Final expense insurance: small whole life policies meant to cover funeral costs

b.tip: For your family, the type matters less than knowing the policy exists. The insurer's name and policy number are what they'll need.

t: Do you have life insurance through work?
pre: Many people do and don't know it.

b.p: Many employers include basic life insurance as a benefit, often at no cost to you. Because it's set up automatically, it's easy to forget about, and families sometimes don't know to claim it.

list: Your employer's benefits portal or open enrollment materials
Your pay stub, which may list life insurance as a deduction or benefit
Your HR department
Coverage is often a flat amount or one to two times your salary.
You may be able to buy extra coverage for yourself or your family.
It usually has its own beneficiary form, separate from any personal policy.

b.p: Work coverage usually ends when employment ends. Some plans let you keep it by converting it to an individual policy or paying for it yourself, within a short window after you leave, often around 31 days, depending on the plan.

b.tip: Under IRS rules, employer-paid coverage above $50,000 counts as taxable income. Coverage above that amount shows up on the W-2 in Box 12 with code C. Coverage of $50,000 or less doesn't appear on the W-2, so the benefits portal or HR is the surer way to check.

t: How to replace a birth certificate or Social Security card
pre: Both can be replaced. One is usually faster than you'd think.

b.p: Missing documents are common. Many people find their birth certificate or Social Security card only when they need it. Both can be replaced, and the process is usually simpler than people expect.

Birth certificates come from the vital records office in the state where you were born, not the state where you live now. Most states take orders online, by mail or in person. Fees usually range from about $10 to $35 per copy, and processing time varies by state.
Searching "[state you were born in] vital records" finds the official office. The CDC also keeps a list of every state's vital records office, with links.

Replacement cards from the Social Security Administration are free. Many adults can request one online through a my Social Security account at ssa.gov, depending on their state and whether they can verify their identity online. Others apply by mail or at a local office.

list: The SSA generally limits replacements to 3 cards a year and 10 in a lifetime, with some exceptions.
Many people rarely need the physical card. Knowing the number is usually enough.

b.p: Some websites charge extra fees to "help" order these documents. The official sources are your birth state's vital records office and ssa.gov.

b.tip: If you're born outside the US to American parents, the record is usually a Consular Report of Birth Abroad, which comes from the State Department instead.

current.label: Replacement Social Security cards per year
Replacement Social Security cards per lifetime

t: Should copies of your ID go in the binder?
pre: Copies can help. The originals usually stay put.

b.p: After a death, family members are often asked for details from the person's ID: full legal name, date of birth, driver's license number, passport number. Having copies nearby can save a search.

b.h: What people commonly keep copies of

list: Driver's license or state ID, front and back
Passport photo page
Medicare and health insurance cards
Military discharge papers (DD-214), if the person served
The original Social Security card, which many people store somewhere secure rather than carrying it
Original birth certificates and passports
Any document with a full Social Security number

b.p: Copies are useful for your family and also useful to anyone who shouldn't have them. Some people mark copies "COPY" across the front, and many keep the binder somewhere out of sight.

A photocopy usually can't replace the original. Agencies like the DMV or passport office typically ask for the original or a certified copy: an official copy ordered from the office that issued the document, with a raised or printed seal.

b.tip: Veterans' families often need the DD-214 for burial benefits. If it's lost, it can usually be requested free from the National Archives.

t: How many years of tax returns to keep
pre: Three years covers most people. Some keep seven.

b.p: After a death, someone usually files a final tax return, and sometimes a return for the estate too. Past returns help them see what income and accounts the person had.

list: The IRS can usually review a return for 3 years after it's filed.
That window becomes 6 years if more than 25% of income was left off the return.
Records for a claim about worthless securities or bad debt are kept for 7 years.
Records about property, like a home, are usually kept until a few years after it's sold.

b.p: A common approach is the last 3 years of returns, with 7 years for anyone who wants extra margin. Records about a house, like the purchase price and improvements, are often kept as long as the house is owned.
Free tax transcripts covering recent years are available from the IRS online or by mail. A family member handling an estate can usually request them with the right paperwork.

b.tip: State rules can differ from the IRS. Some states can review returns for longer than 3 years.

current.label: Worthless securities or bad debt records

t: Keeping your binder secure: where to store it and who gets access
pre: Safe enough to protect it. Easy enough for family to find.

b.p: A binder full of account details needs some protection. But a binder no one can reach doesn't help either. Most families look for a middle ground.

table: Protected, easy for family to reach
Someone needs the code or key
Family may not be able to open it quickly after a death; rules vary by state and bank
They need to keep it safe too

b.p: Many people tell one or two people where the binder is and how to get to it: often the executor, a spouse, or an adult child. Telling them now saves them a search later.

If the templates are kept in Google Drive, the Drive account becomes part of the plan. Many people share the folder with one trusted person, or make sure that person can get into the account through Google's Inactive Account Manager.

b.tip: A short note on the first page of the binder, saying where the originals are kept, helps whoever opens it.

t: How to write a letter to your family
pre: There's no wrong way. Short is fine.

b.p: A letter isn't a legal document. It's the part of the plan your family may read the most. Many people put off writing one because they don't know what to say. Most letters that families treasure are simple.

list: What each person has meant to them
A favorite memory or two
Hopes for their family's future
Anything they want to explain, apologize for or let go of
Small practical wishes, like a favorite song for a service
Writing a few lines at a time, over several days
Writing one short letter to each person instead of one long one
Recording a voice memo or video instead of writing
Using a prompt, like "The thing I most want you to know is…"

b.p: Some people worry their letter will be too sad. Families often say the letters they value most sound like the person: funny, plain or a little messy. Perfect isn't the point.
Some people call this an ethical will or a legacy letter. These aren't legally binding, and they can sit alongside a will.

b.tip: People often update their letters after big life events. Dating each one helps your family know which is the latest.

t: Cloud photos: making sure they aren't lost
pre: Your photos may be in one account no one else can open.

b.p: For many people, the family photo album now lives in a phone or a cloud account. If no one can get into that account, the photos can be very hard to recover.

list: iCloud Photos (iPhone)
Google Photos (Android or the app)
Amazon Photos, Dropbox or OneDrive
A computer or external hard drive
Social media accounts

b.h: Tools that let family get in

list: Apple Legacy Contact: someone you choose can request access to your Apple account data, including photos, messages, notes and files, after your death. It doesn't include purchased movies, music or books, or saved passwords.
Google Inactive Account Manager: you choose who gets your Google Photos and other data if your account goes unused for a set time.

Facebook legacy contact: someone you choose can manage a memorialized account and download the photos, videos and posts you shared, if you allowed it. It doesn't include messages, or photos that were synced but never posted.
Sharing a family album, so others already have copies
Downloading favorites to a hard drive once or twice a year
Printing a small book of the most important photos

b.tip: Apple and Google both have rules about how long they keep data from inactive accounts. Setting up a legacy contact now is much easier than requesting access later.

t: Is a "who gets what" list legally binding?
pre: Usually not on its own. But it can still help.

b.p: Many people make a list of who gets the watch, the china or the quilt. Whether that list counts legally depends on your state and how it connects to your will.

list: A list on its own, with no will, is usually not legally binding. Your state's default rules decide who inherits.

About half of US states let a will refer to a separate written list of personal belongings, often called a tangible personal property memorandum. If the will mentions it, the list can be binding in those states.
Even where it's allowed, the list usually covers only personal belongings, not money, houses, cars with titles or bank accounts.

b.p: Even when a list isn't binding, families often follow it. It shows what the person wanted and can head off disagreements over things that matter for sentimental reasons.

b.h: Things that help a list hold up

list: Signing and dating it
Describing items clearly, like "Grandma's silver watch" rather than "the watch"
Keeping it with the will
Updating it when items are sold or given away

b.tip: Rules vary by state. Searching "[your state] personal property memorandum" shows whether your state allows one.
